text: The ropewalk closed the following spring. Its last order book is full to the final page, with orders for rope it would never make. Did the owner know, when he wrote them in, that he would not be able to fill them?
strengths: the order book is a strong final piece of evidence
the question is one the film genuinely cannot answer
weaknesses: ending on a question hands the last beat to speculation
spokenRhythm: A short statement, a medium one that sets the evidence, and a longer question with an interrupting clause.
narrativeFunction: Leaves the audience with the owner's state of mind at the close of the business.
whyItWorks: A single question at the very end can work when the evidence has been laid out and the record truly falls silent. It invites the audience to weigh the order book for themselves.
whyItFails: The closing question is the reflex ending of machine-written history, and it can sound like a hook for a sequel. It also nudges the audience toward a dramatic reading the record does not support. The same uncertainty, said as a statement, ends the film more confidently.
rewrite: The ropewalk closed the following spring. Its last order book is full to the final page, with orders for rope it would never make. The book doesn't say whether the owner knew, when he wrote them in, that he could not fill them.

text: The tolls on the bridge were abolished forty years after it opened. In all that time, the charge for a man crossing on foot had stayed at a penny. Some things on the river never moved.
strengths: the penny that never rose is a genuinely funny fact
the two figures sit in separate sentences
weaknesses: the last line explains its own joke
the closing frame is a twist on the saying that some things never change
spokenRhythm: Two plain factual sentences, then a short line that asks for a smile.
narrativeFunction: Closes a film about a toll bridge on a fact that sums up its unchanging business.
whyItWorks: The penny that never rose is already funny, and one short dry line after it can send an audience out smiling when the film has been light on its feet throughout. The play on moved is quiet, and it is the only joke the ending makes.
whyItFails: The line explains a joke the facts have already made, and its frame is a stock saying in disguise. A film that closes its sections this way soon has a sign-off formula, and the endings start to sound alike. Most of the time, cut it and let the penny land on its own.
rewrite: The tolls on the bridge were abolished forty years after it opened. In all that time, the charge for a man crossing on foot had stayed at a penny.

text: The guild did not end in a crisis. It ended at a dinner, with a vote by members who wanted the hall for something else. The minutes record the motion, the count, and the cost of the wine.
strengths: the anticlimax is the point and the record supplies it
the last sentence lets the wine make the joke
spokenRhythm: A short negation, a longer correction, and a list of three that closes on the dry detail.
narrativeFunction: Ends a film about a medieval guild by correcting the dramatic end the audience may expect.
whyItWorks: Used once, a negation can correct an expectation the film has genuinely built, and here the correction is a plain, slightly comic fact from the minutes.
whyItFails: The not-this-but-that shape is among the most recognisable machine habits. It fails if the film has used it before, or if nobody in the audience was expecting a crisis in the first place. Without the negation the ending loses nothing.
rewrite: The guild ended at a dinner, with a vote by members who wanted the hall for something else. The minutes record the motion, the count, and the cost of the wine.
